description: Source-lore pass 15 imports airship crew scaling, supply usage, weekly travel roles, failure pressure, and morale.

entries.title: Airship Crews and Supplies
entries.summary: Crew specialization, food, water, fuel, wages, ammunition, and operating cost rise dramatically from a one-pilot Jetty to a Dreadnought with hundreds aboard.
body: Airship crews grow with vessel scale and mission complexity. A Jetty may combine captain, engineer, cook, and maintenance work in one person. Scutters add general hands and security. Corvettes and Frigates separate captains, engineers, gunners, cooks, quartermasters, lookouts, and maintenance crews.

Cruisers and Liners require multiple engineers, gunners, cooks, quartermasters, lookouts, freight handlers, and passenger stewards. Destroyers add marines and larger combat departments. Galleons, Battleships, and Dreadnoughts operate as communities with extensive engineering, artillery, stores, lookout, marine, kitchen, cargo, and command staff.

Propulsion and supply also scale. Small vessels use wind, steam, coal, or enchanted crystals; larger ships rely on advanced etheric or hybrid engines and consume many barrels of fuel each week. Food, [[water-in-the-skies|water]], wages, parts, and ammunition make large ships expensive to keep moving even when no battle occurs.

Range is therefore not merely a speed statistic. It depends on crew competence, stores, fuel, maintenance, route conditions, cargo load, and whether the vessel can reach a port capable of supporting its class.

sections.heading: Legacy Crew and Cost Tables
body: The source lists crew departments, fuel barrels, ration rates, supply duration, daily range, and daily gold costs for every class from Jetty to Dreadnought. Some ration figures appear internally inconsistent and require normalization during conversion.

entries.title: Airship Travel Roles
entries.summary: Weekly voyages depend on command, engineering, navigation, quartermastering, cooking, morale, repairs, freight handling, security, and discipline.
body: A successful airship voyage is collective work. The captain coordinates orders and leadership; engineers maintain propulsion; navigators hold the route; quartermasters manage food, water, and cargo; cooks protect health; and designated crew maintain morale.

Carpenters and smiths prevent minor damage from becoming structural failure. Freight crews balance and secure cargo. Security watches detect sabotage, boarders, creatures, and harbor threats. Officers or trusted veterans keep disputes from escalating into theft, violence, or breakdown of discipline.

Failure spreads between departments. Poor navigation creates delays and hazards; bad stores management causes hunger and disease; neglected engines reduce speed or consume fuel; weak security invites theft and boarding; damaged cargo changes balance and maneuverability; repeated leadership failures drive [[crew-morale|morale]] toward mutiny.

sections.heading: Legacy Weekly Checks
body: The source provides skills, DCs, and numerical consequences for ten weekly roles. These require conversion, but the role structure is preserved.

entries.title: Airship Crew Morale
entries.summary: Morale determines whether an airship crew works with exceptional efficiency, makes costly mistakes, sabotages operations, rebels, or mutinies.
body: Morale affects every department aboard an airship. A trusted, rested, fairly supplied crew coordinates navigation, repairs, cooking, cargo, and battle work efficiently. Neutral morale produces ordinary performance; declining morale introduces mistakes, delays, arguments, neglect, and sabotage.

Severe discontent spreads from individual grievances into open rebellion. At the lowest point, routine command collapses and mutiny becomes likely unless leadership addresses the crew's conditions immediately.

Positive morale comes from fair pay, adequate food and [[water-in-the-skies|water]], successful voyages, rest, recognition, entertainment, competent command, and visible concern for safety. Negative morale grows through shortages, overwork, danger without purpose, unfair discipline, unpaid wages, failed leadership, casualties, and repeated technical disasters.

Morale cannot be repaired only through threats. Celebrations, shore leave, improved quarters, shared profit, honest explanation, replacing abusive officers, resolving grievances, and completing meaningful goals can restore trust.

sections.heading: Legacy Morale Scale
body: The source uses a scale from +10 highly positive morale through 0 neutral to -20 mutinous, with escalating roll modifiers, sabotage, rebellion, and mutiny. Conversion is required.

sourceRefs.outlineTitle: Crew Morale Effects on Ship Performance
